Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Vignette:
Elias Vance spent nearly two decades shaping lecture halls and grading seminar papers, his life organized around academic rhythms, until a weekend mountain trip in western Virginia unraveled his sense of safety. He had been hiking with his nineteen-year-old nephew, Julian, along a dry creek bed when a sudden, violent downpour sent a wall of flash flood water tearing through the gorge. Elias reached for him, but the current swallowed Julian’s hand and dragged him downstream before Elias could plant his boots. The memory does not arrive as a coherent narrative so much as a sudden physical collapse. When Elias closes his eyes, he is still knee-deep in the churning brown current, the metallic tang of flooded soil and wet pine filling his nose. He remembers the precise drag of the water against his chest, the way the river roared in his ears, and the hollow, silent waiting that followed when Julian did not surface. Since that afternoon, Elias’s daily environment has become a landscape of careful navigation. He no longer walks past the campus reflecting pool near the humanities building without a sudden, suffocating lurch in his throat. The sight of rain pooling in the courtyard gutters, the sound of the department’s aquarium venting in the graduate office, even the faint, damp-earth scent that clings to his office chair after a heavy storm—all of it short-circuits his nervous system. His body reacts to danger before he has even had time to think. In faculty meetings, when the overhead sprinklers test during a summer heatwave, his heart hammers against his ribs, his palms slick, his breath coming in shallow pulls before his mind can register that he is simply sitting in a climate-controlled room. He has come to believe that the water remembers what it took, and that it will return if he ever stops watching. The weeks and months following the flood brought a quiet accumulation of retreat. Elias stopped taking the scenic route past the river trail behind the science buildings. He canceled trips to the coast, opting instead for inland conferences where the nearest body of water was a municipal drinking fountain. He told himself it was practical, that he simply needed a more efficient schedule, but he recognized the underlying mechanism. When the water finally did reach him, whether through a sudden downpour or the sharp, petrichor scent of a breaking storm, strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame would rise in his chest, unbidden and inescapable. He was certain that if he allowed himself to feel the full weight of what happened, he would fracture completely, so he built routines around his grief. Even in the sanctuary of his own home, Elias cannot relax. He lies awake long after midnight, muscles coiled, listening to the hum of the refrigerator and the distant drip of a faucet, convinced that safety is merely a temporary pause. In his professorship, the sheer volume of student emails and departmental deadlines triggers a paralyzing stress that makes his vision tunnel. He has started declining committee appointments, claiming a heavy teaching load, when in truth he cannot bear the prospect of another unpredictable demand. He is alone, living in a meticulously ordered apartment that has become less a home and more a buffer against the world. What finally brought Elias to your office was not a breaking point, but a slow erosion. Last week, a campus maintenance crew opened a storm drain near his office, releasing a gush of rainwater onto the pavement. The sound alone sent him from the building, his hands shaking, unable to return until the afternoon lecture was over. He sat in his car, staring at the steering wheel, certain that he had lost his mind, and desperate to understand why the past would not let him teach. He is seeking help not because he hopes the memories will fade, but because he wants to know how to stand in a room full of students without feeling the ground turn to water beneath his feet, and how to finally rest.
